We've been using Zulip internally for a couple of years now... It lets us have real, ongoing, and substantive conversations with a large number of participants without being overwhelmed. Twitter is actually a better comparison for Zulip than Slack.
No linux client? That's a deal breaker for us right there... Pity, looks interesting otherwise.
Something has gone horribly wrong when a chat server can barely run on 2G... recommended 4GB of RAM for production use.
Good to see it be open sourced. I'm disappointed there's no XMPP gateway, OTR chat encryption or Gitlab integration however.
The 'threaded' part is key here. Slack threads are useless compared to Zulip. In Zulip you can create threads on the fly from existing messages... fundamentally superior model.
Zulip's threading model encourages long-form, more forum or email like discussions... The only downside is the very subpar UX when compared to Discord or even Slack.
Zulip has a notoriously bad db schema. For example, a single write in a 5000 member public group would result in 5000 writes to the user table.
Zulip is my favorite modern chat program because it's actually 100% FOSS, unlike Mattermost and RocketChat, which are only 'open core'.

I use Zulip all the time at work. It is ugly, sometimes will post to a different thread than you expect... has an infuriating tick that if you click off the input box, it deletes everything you typed.

Zulip seemed like technically the most polished product... what ended up being the showstopper was that new users were very confused about how to write in a channel. Non-technical users had a really hard time.
We used Zulip (then a commercial product) at FoundationDB, and really liked it... the killer feature is the 'all messages' view that merges chosen streams in more or less chronological order.
It's very expensive compared to slack though. I thought it would be priced closer to the cheaper alternatives.

I love Zulip... what Zulip lacks right now is polish. Server installation for example is a mess. You basically need a dedicated Debian machine to install it... search function barely works, lacks archiving topics.

The install procedure looks like a bad joke. So if I'm using RHEL, Fedora, Arch or any other Linux distribution, tough luck. If they're supporting only Ubuntu, they could have at least created some deb packages.
Threads are one major reason I like Zulip over Slack, but speed is another... For some reason when I use Slack, the keys feel mushy.
A group of us in the Julia open source community have been trying to migrate to Zulip from Slack... The topics model is fantastic, having proper markdown and LaTeX support is also killer.

My research group at Stanford uses Zulip... In the time since I have switched from Slack to Zulip (about 1 year ago now), Slack has gone down 3-4 times and has had other connectivity issues; Zulip had maybe 1-2 minor interruptions.
On the downside, if you are self-hosting, Zulip requires a dedicated server (or VM). There are some efforts to make it run in a container but nothing that works really well.
Tried to convert some non-techie business types to using Zulip. Was really difficult to get them to understand streams and threading... the instance on DO ended up a ghost town.
I used Zulip while at Akamai... My experience was so positive that I've continued to evangelize it at other companies since then... The most important feature of Zulip is threading.
